Consult the Oracle 4.4 Titan Attack 5 Recolouring 6 Actions 6.1 Any Colour 6.2 Colour Must Match 6.3 Fighting a Monster 6.4 Exploring an Island 7 Task Rewards 8 Gods 9 Companion Cards 10 Ship Tiles 11 Ending the Game 12 FAQ Overview Welcome to the Oracle of Delphi where you will perform the twelve tasks given to you by Zeus. Those tasks involve collecting offerings and delivering them to their corresponding temples, transporting statues to be raised on designated islands, discovering hidden islands to build temples and slaying monsters. Goal Complete your 12 Zeus tasks, then sail back to Zeus at the centre of the board. The first player to return triggers the end. The round finishes, then the game ends. Task Count How Shrine 3 Build a Shrine on an Island Tile showing your player colour Offering 3 Load an Offering cube, deliver it to the Temple of that colour Statue 3 Load a Statue at a City, raise it on a Statue Island of that colour Monster 3 Defeat a Monster of the colour shown on the tile White icons on a Zeus Tile mean "any colour", but no colour can repeat within one task type. You may not fight Monsters or load Offerings or Statues that no remaining task needs. Colours Six colours run through everything: dice, water spaces, islands, Gods, Monsters, Offerings, Statues and Injury Cards. Colour Symbol God Monster Red Aphrodite Cyclops Black Ares Minotaur Pink Hermes Hydra Blue Poseidon Siren Yellow Apollo Chimera Green Artemis Gorgon The table follows the oracle wheel in clockwise order: red, black, pink, blue, yellow, green, back to red. Turn Structure 1. Check Injuries Your Injury Cards Result 3 of one colour, or 6 total Recover: discard any 3, skip the rest of your turn, do not roll 0 Take 2 Favor Tokens or advance 1 God 1 step Anything else Nothing happens 2. Take Actions Use these in any order: 3 Oracle Dice : each die gives one action of its colour. 1 Oracle Card : at most one per turn, used like a die. God Special Actions : any God on the top row of your God Track. No die needed. Finish each action before starting the next. 3. Consult the Oracle Roll your 3 dice. Those colours are your dice for next turn. Every other player with a God of a rolled colour above the bottom row may advance one such God 1 step. You never advance your own Gods from your own roll. Titan Attack The last player in turn order rolls the Titan's Die along with their dice, even if they Recovered. Titan rolls 6: every player draws 2 Injury Cards. Otherwise: each player whose Shield is lower than the Titan roll draws 1 Injury Card. Recolouring Before using a die or Oracle Card, move it clockwise around the wheel for 1 Favor Token per step. Example: green to red is 1 step, red to green is 5 steps. Actions Any Colour Action Effect Draw Oracle Card Draw 1 Oracle Card. No hand limit. Take Favor Take 2 Favor Tokens Peek Look at 2 face-down Island Tiles, then return them face down Colour Must Match Island and City actions require your Ship to be adjacent to that space. Action Effect Move Ship Move up to 3 water spaces and end on a space of the die colour. Pay 1 Favor per extra space. Cannot cross islands or shallows. Fight Monster Fight the Monster of the die colour on an adjacent island. It does not need to be on top of the stack. Explore Island Flip the adjacent face-down Island Tile with a matching hex colour and take its reward Build Shrine Place a Shrine on an uncovered Island Tile

[Rating: 1/10] Roll and move, pick up and deliver and lots of randomness.  It doesn't gel together for me.  Very different from the earlier Feld's which I like.

[Rating: 2/10] Pick up and deliver game with a modular board, with a color scheme (colored action dice, colored cubes and statues to deliver, colored spaces and temples to deliver to, colored monsters to fight with dice), special abilities, punishing cards, helper cards and a race element.  Very complicated for what it is, i have not seen a euro with this many components, and I find the luck element too much for this complexity. Not the best game of Herr Feld

[Rating: 2/10] This is a pickup and deliver game where each turn you roll three dice, and the dice determine your success or failure in terms of being able to make efficient moves. Each round a penalty die is rolled, and if you didn't prepare proper defenses, you take a wound card. Once you have a certain number of those cards, you have to skip a turn which can be harsh. The game has a lot of different ways to mitigate your luck, and some engine building which is nice, but ultimately it's a competent but uninspiring efficiency game. [Rating: 2/10] Bad gameplay, skipping a turn should not be part of modern games. Had to skip a turn twice in a row.

[Rating: 2/10] Chaotic pick up and deliver. This was one of the most Ameritrash-y feeling games I've ever played. I think pick up and deliver generally isn't my jam, but throwing in the chaos of the dice rolling tipped this one off the cliff for me. There is moderate amounts of mitigation, but it never feels like enough, and the fact that you're competing against the game and not other people means you can't even enjoy the table talk of reveling in others' detriment to your success.  +Semi-mythological theming is a bit of a twist on the classic "trading on the Mediterranean." +Dice rondel is a fun action sel

[Rating: 3/10] Definitely my least favorite Feld. I don't usually mind a bit of luck in games, but in Oracle of Delphi the pure Luck of the roll to resolve mechanism completely ruined my chance of enjoying the game.

[Rating: 3/10] [Played once]  A race (no real intereaction) to accomplish a variety of tasks, with abundant luck attached and a variety of special powers to add complexity to a simple game (too convoluted if you want something simple, too bland if you want something deep).  Unoriginal and worse than its average ilk.

[Rating: 3/10] Wow, this was play tested? I don't think so!  Highly unbalanced skills and way too much  luck involved.  And it's really ugly.

[Rating: 3/10] Set in Ancient Greece, you have 12 objectives of four different types you have to complete by matching the colors on the dice you roll to the spaces or resources or monsters on the board. I normally like Stefan Feld games, but I felt I saw everything I needed to see in about twenty minutes of the game and wanted it to end. It's extremely luck-driven, and while there are ways to mitigate that luck, most of that mitigation is granted as you complete objectives, so what can happen (and did happen for me) is that a couple people accomplished several objectives and started having all sorts of wilds

[Rating: 3/10] Absolutely not a game for me. In essence a race (meta) game with too much stuff jammed in. Too much randomness, too much downtime, too much fog in the rules and not nearly enough interaction.

[Rating: 3/10] Midway through I started to really dislike this game.  The game-play is frustrating and zero fun.  I usually like Feld's efforts, but not this time.  Bad.

[Rating: 3/10] I think I might not like race games. Even though all the mechanisms were proper feldian, this one just didn't spark any excitement. Properly balanced though, every game that I remember was really close.

[Rating: 3/10] Some good stuff in  the game including god powers, unique starting abilities with the ship, lots of variety with the map setup, optional goals, solid dice mitigation strategies. However, as a whole, very meh feeling with this one. I found a lot of it just didn't work:  1) Fiddly setup and general arc of play feels... messy. I think it's kind of intended to feel somewhat chaotic, but it means you're being pushed by the game rather than playing the game. 2) Every turn is either obvious or lackluster.
